articles.title: The F-Pattern: When It Happens, and How to Design Around It
articles.summary: The F-pattern is one of the most cited and most misunderstood findings in web usability. The research shows it is a fallback for badly formatted text, and that good design can steer attention elsewhere.

sections.heading: Where the F-pattern came from
sections.body: In 2006, Jakob Nielsen at Nielsen Norman Group reported an eyetracking study of 232 users. Heatmaps showed a sweep across the top, a shorter second sweep, then a scan down the left edge. His advice: put the key information in the first two paragraphs and start headings and bullets with informative words.

sections.body: A 2007 Wichita State study confirmed the F-pattern on text pages but found image-based pages produced a more uniform scan, with fixations on images dropping sharply near and below the fold. A small 2009 study found faces below the fold drew attention to nearby text.

articles.body:
If you have read anything about landing page design, you have met the F-pattern. It is one of the most cited findings in web usability, and one of the most misunderstood. Here is what the research actually says.

## Where the F-pattern came from

In 2006, Jakob Nielsen at Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g) reported an eyetracking study of 232 users looking at thousands of web pages. Heatmaps of an about-us article, an e-commerce product page and a search results page all showed a similar shape: a horizontal sweep across the top of the content, a shorter second sweep lower down, and then a vertical scan along the left edge. Nielsen's advice was practical: put the most important information in the first two paragraphs, and start subheads, paragraphs and bullets with information-carrying words, because people read the first couple of words much more than the third.

## It is a fallback, not a law

Kara Pernice's 2017 follow-up, based on new eyetracking research, corrected common misreadings. People do not always scan in an F. NN/g found the pattern appears when three things are true at once: the text has little web formatting (a wall of text with no bold, bullets or subheadings), the reader is trying to be efficient, and the reader is not so interested that they will read every word. In other words, the F is what people fall back on when the page gives their eyes no better cues. It appeared on mobile screens too, and in Arabic, a right-to-left language, it was mirrored.

Pernice also calls the F-pattern bad for both users and businesses, because people skip large chunks of content, often including things that matter, without knowing it. Her recommended antidotes are ordinary good formatting: key points in the first two paragraphs, visible subheadings that start with informative words, grouped content, bold key phrases, and bullets or numbers for lists.

## Other researchers found the same limits

A 2007 study from Wichita State University's usability lab (Shrestha, Lenz, Owens and Chaparro) tracked eyes on text-based and image-based pages of an e-commerce site. The F-pattern showed up on text pages during both browsing and searching. On image-based pages, browsers followed a fairly uniform scan path and looked more at images above the fold, with fixations dropping sharply on images near and below the fold.

A 2009 study by Soussan Djamasbi and colleagues went further. They gave 34 participants two versions of a financial company's homepage prototype that differed in one below-the-fold section: one included images of faces, the other did not. Content above the fold still drew the most fixations overall, but the faces acted as entry points, pulling fixations to the text beside them even below the fold. Their conclusion was that a richer visual hierarchy can guide attention outside the F. The study was small, and it was a short conference paper, so treat it as a promising signal rather than settled fact.

## What to do on a landing page

Use the F-pattern as a warning sign rather than a template. Where you have running text, front-load it and format it so people can find their way. Where you have images, make sure the most informative ones sit high on the page. And where you want attention below the fold, give the eye a visible entry point, such as a clear heading or a relevant image, instead of hoping people will read down the left edge.

articles.title: Z-Patterns, Zigzags and Columns: What the Evidence Says About Layout Shapes
articles.summary: The Z-pattern is popular but has no web eyetracking evidence we could find, while zigzag layouts and two-column text have been tested. Here is what held up.

sections.heading: The Z-pattern: popular, but unsupported
sections.body: We could not trace the Z-pattern to any web eyetracking study. It appears to come from the print-era Gutenberg diagram. NN/g's research supports top and left attention, an F-shaped fallback on unformatted text, and efficient scanning when headings are clear.

sections.body: In NN/g's 2017 study, informational images were studied in both zigzag and aligned layouts. Decorative images were ignored, and in zigzag rows the eye kept stumbling onto them. Align decorative images and keep zigzags short.

sections.heading: Columns: helpful, with limits
sections.body: A 2008 study found information in a second column got more fixations than the same information lower in a single column, and that the F-pattern appeared in the left column but not the right.

sections.body: Prefer aligned rows unless every image earns its place, use Z-shaped compositions as a heuristic rather than a rule, and place high-information content on the left.

articles.body:
The F-pattern has decades of eyetracking behind it. Its cousins, the Z-pattern and the zigzag layout, are not on equal footing. Here is what we could and could not verify.

## The Z-pattern: popular, but unsupported

Z-pattern advice says that on sparse pages people scan from the top left to the top right, cut diagonally down to the bottom left, and then sweep to the bottom right, so you should put your logo, navigation and calls to action at the corners of that path. It is repeated across design blogs, but we could not trace it to any web eyetracking study. It appears to be borrowed from the print-era Gutenberg diagram, which was designed for evenly distributed text, not for modern pages. NN/g's eyetracking work instead supports a different picture: attention concentrated at the top and on the left (Fessenden, 2017), an F-shaped fallback on unformatted text (Nielsen, 2006; Pernice, 2017), and efficient scanning when clear headings exist (Pernice, 2019). So if you use a Z-shaped composition, treat it as a design heuristic that gives a page a tidy structure, not as research.

## Zigzag layouts: tested, with a catch

A layout that does have evidence is the zigzag: rows where an image alternates between the left and right side of the text. Kim Flaherty (2017, NN/g) compared zigzag and aligned versions of four real pages (Splitwise, Waze, HelloFresh and BoxyCharm), with about 30 to 35 participants per version.

When images carried real information, such as product photos people needed to understand what they were buying, both layouts worked about equally well. People studied those images no matter where they sat. The trouble came with decorative images. Users learned quickly to ignore them, and in the zigzag layout their eyes kept stumbling onto the images as they scrolled, then jumping back to the text. NN/g argues that these accidental fixations add up like clutter in an untidy room. Overly complex images, such as screenshots full of tiny text, were also skipped when they appeared too early.

NN/g's advice is to align decorative images down one side, top-align them with their text, keep zigzag for short sequences of two or three rows or for genuinely informative images, and put high-information content on the left of the first row.

## Columns: helpful, with limits

Two-column text layouts show a related pattern. In a 2008 Wichita State study, Shrestha, Owens and Chaparro found that information in a second column got more fixations than the same information placed lower in a single column, and that the F-shaped pattern appeared in the left column but not the right. They also saw more fixations on ads among people who were browsing than among those searching for something. This was a short conference presentation on text pages, so it suggests rather than proves, but the takeaway is sensible: a second column can lift secondary content into view, yet it should not be expected to be scanned like the main column.

## Practical guidance

Choose aligned rows unless every image earns its place. Use zigzags sparingly, and check that each image tells the visitor something. Use a Z-shaped composition if you like how it looks, but do not rely on it to steer attention.

articles.title: The Fold: Where Attention Really Drops Off
articles.summary: Lab eyetracking says attention falls sharply at the fold, while analytics from news sites say readers spend most of their time below it. Both are true, and together they give a workable rule for the first screen.

articles.body:
'Above the fold' is a newspaper term that has been declared dead and alive again several times. The evidence explains why both camps sound convincing.

## The case that the fold still matters

Amy Schade's 2015 'Fold Manifesto' at Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g) argued that the fold still exists on every device, even though its exact position varies. In an analysis of 57,453 eyetracking fixations, the 100 pixels just above the fold were viewed 102% more than the 100 pixels just below it. She also cited Google's analysis of display ads, where ads just above the fold were viewable 73% of the time and ads just below only 44%, a 66% drop. NN/g took the midpoint of the two and concluded that users treat content above and below the fold about 84% differently. The reasoning is about effort: what is visible costs nothing to see, while what needs scrolling costs a little effort, so people scroll only when the top of the page gives them a reason.

## Scrolling has grown, but attention still decays

Therese Fessenden's 2018 update at NN/g analyzed more than 130,000 fixations from 120 participants on larger screens. About 57% of viewing time was above the fold, down from 80% in 2010, and 74% fell within the first two screenfuls. In effect the barrier had moved: 81% of viewing time was spent within the first three screenfuls, and people rarely went beyond that. The pattern of sharp drop-off after the fold was the same as in 2010. Her recommendations were to reserve the top for key business and user goals, keep major calls to action above the fold, and beware 'false floors' that make a page look finished.

## The counterpoint from analytics

In 2014, Chartbeat CEO Tony Haile wrote in Time that, across roughly 2 billion visits, about 66% of attention on a normal media page was spent below the fold. This seems to contradict NN/g, but the two measure different things and different pages. Chartbeat's data comes from analytics on mostly news and media article pages, where a likely reason for deep scrolling is that readers who have chosen a story keep reading it. NN/g's data comes from lab eyetracking across tasks and site types, where visitors are still deciding whether the page is relevant. Neither dataset is about landing pages specifically.

## What it means for landing pages

Reconciling the sources gives a sensible working rule. The first screen decides whether people keep going, so it needs your value proposition and your main call to action. But below the fold is not dead space: visitors who are interested will scroll, and they will spend real time there if the page keeps giving them reasons. Design each section to earn the next scroll, use signposts such as anchor links on long pages, and check your own analytics, because your visitors may behave differently from news readers or lab participants.
